e-8249.knowledge_point: Finding the Canonical Form of a Quadratic Function by Finding Eigenvalues
e-8249.problem: Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of $Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2+x_2^2+2x_3^2+4x_1x_2.$
e-8249.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/44753acffd8b6384cd291f9b0758edd7676acb319caa22d5b07be36dcf72a5a6.png)

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(\lambda -3)(\lambda +1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,2,\,-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/217b5d7d3b82800bdfc44d83ca8b068e02a37759e52b7a8382505bfb102f753f.png)

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
3y_1^2 + 2y_2^2 - y_3^2.
$$

e-8250.knowledge_point: Reducing a Quadratic Function Over the 2D-Space to the Canonical Form Using Orthogonal Transformations
e-8250.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=2x_1^2-2x_1x_2+2x_2^2,$ find its canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
e-8250.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/69dcf821f3ff202b567b901d8f512c5cecf7159617ca51a0664c14a5099e9715.png)

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +3 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For $\lambda_1=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/fc9465d4e5bcd43a3c29e5946b05ec18cdbc7453a4011aa548f374016c561b45.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/59c1bd46325fab8a52fed162d7ae47e8fb33a10cc524cd770a3b18f5934e51dd.png)

- For $\lambda_2=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/adc9241219f3b5ebce0d8418bf34e250b7230ea612fabca5bdfc109c98a18dbb.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/dcab437eb77b29ab5bcd5c3ae14b77f10f01382aafadf2aecded1bb1fb72dc32.png)

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/3f6b1002893290dde6c9a68425b0035e249ff3630a41d29c9da5756c1a18f6a6.png)

decision.explanation: The symmetric matrix is A = [[1,0,2],[0,1,0],[2,0,1]]. Its eigenvalues are 3, 1, and -1, so orthogonal diagonalization gives 3y_1^2+y_2^2-y_3^2.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{3}.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(\lambda -3)(\lambda +1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,1,\,-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
3{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}-{y}_{3}^{2}.
$$

Question 1
?

Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of Q(x)=x12+x22+x32+4x1x3.

a
3y12+y32
b
y12+y22+y32
c
3y12+y22−y32
d
y12−y22
e
2y12−y22−y32
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[102010201]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of A:

|A−λI|=0|1−λ0201−λ0201−λ|=0(1−λ)|1−λ221−λ|=0(1−λ)((1−λ)(1−λ)−4)=0(1−λ)(λ2−2λ−3)=0(1−λ)(λ−3)(λ+1)=0λ=3,1,−1

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

D=[30001000−1].

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

3y12+y22−y32.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Canonical Form of a Quadratic Function by Finding Eigenvalues
content.problem: Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{3}.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(\lambda -3)(\lambda +1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,1,\,-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
3{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}-{y}_{3}^{2}.
$$

decision.explanation: The symmetric matrix is A = [[1,3],[3,1]]. Its characteristic equation is (1-λ)^2-9=0, giving eigenvalues 4 and -2. Thus the canonical form is 4y_1^2-2y_2^2.

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]

$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
4{y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{2}^{2}.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[1221]

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of A:

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Canonical Form of a Quadratic Function by Finding Eigenvalues
content.problem: Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda +1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
3{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}.
$$

after.problem: Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -6 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda -3) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
3{y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{2}^{2}.
$$

Question 4
?

Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of Q(x)=−x12+4x1x2+2x22.

a
−2y12−3y22
b
2y12
c
3y12−2y22
d
−3y22
e
3y12+2y22
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[−1222]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of A:

|A−λI|=0|−1−λ222−λ|=0(−1−λ)(2−λ)−4=0λ2−λ−6=0(λ+2)(λ−3)=0λ=3,−2

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

D=[300−2].

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

3y12−2y22.

verification.explanation: For A = [[-1,2],[2,2]], the characteristic polynomial is λ²-λ-6 = (λ-3)(λ+2). Its eigenvalues 3 and -2 give the canonical form 3y_1²-2y_2², confirming option c and the revealed solution. The deliberately incorrect submission selected d.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Canonical Form of a Quadratic Function by Finding Eigenvalues
content.problem: Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -6 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda -3) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
3{y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{2}^{2}.
$$

Question 5
?

Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of Q(x)=x12+x22−x32−6x1x2.

a
y12−y22+2y32
b
4y12−y22−2y32
c
4y12−2y22
d
−y12−2y22−2y32
e
2y12+y22
Submit

decision.explanation: The symmetric matrix is A = [[1,-3,0],[-3,1,0],[0,0,-1]]. The upper 2×2 block has eigenvalues 4 and -2, and the remaining eigenvalue is -1. In descending order, orthogonal diagonalization gives 4y_1²-y_2²-2y_3².

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}-{x}_{3}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-9) & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -8) & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )(\lambda -4)(\lambda +2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,-1,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

A=[1−30−31000−1]

|A−λI|=0|1−λ−30−31−λ000−1−λ|=0(−1−λ)|1−λ−3−31−λ|=0(−1−λ)((1−λ)(1−λ)−9)=0(−1−λ)(λ2−2λ−8)=0(−1−λ)(λ−4)(λ+2)=0λ=4,−1,−2

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Canonical Form of a Quadratic Function by Finding Eigenvalues
content.problem: Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}-{x}_{3}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-9) & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -8) & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )(\lambda -4)(\lambda +2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,-1,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
4{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}-2{y}_{3}^{2}.
$$

Question 6
?

Given the quadratic form Q(x)=2x12−4x1x2+5x22, find its canonical (diagonal) form yTDy and an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables.

a
D=[−1001] and P=[1001]
b
D=[3001] and P=[−12121212]
c
D=[6001] and P=[−15252515]
d
D=[300−2] and P=[−26262626]
e
D=[4002] and P=[−13232313]
Submit

decision.explanation: The matrix A = [[2,-2],[-2,5]] has eigenvalues 6 and 1. Corresponding unit eigenvectors are (-1,2)/√5 and (2,1)/√5. These orthonormal columns form the displayed P in option c, satisfying PᵀAP = D and giving Q = 6y_1²+y_2².

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +6 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =6,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 6

Given the quadratic form Q(x)=2x12−4x1x2+5x22, find its canonical (diagonal) form yTDy and an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables.

a
D=[−1001] and P=[1001]
b
D=[3001] and P=[−12121212]
c
D=[6001] and P=[−15252515]
d
D=[300−2] and P=[−26262626]
e
D=[4002] and P=[−13232313]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[2−2−25]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of A:

|A−λI|=0|2−λ−2−25−λ|=0λ2−7λ+6=0λ=6,1

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=6, we have A−6I=[2−2−25]−6[1001]=[−4−2−2−1]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−6I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[−12]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=5, we get v2‖v2‖=15[−12].

  • For λ2=1, we have A−1I=[2−2−25]−1[1001]=[1−2−24]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−1I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[21]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=5, we get v1‖v1‖=15[21].

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix D (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: D=[6001],P=[−15252515]

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option c. For A = [[2,-2],[-2,5]], the orthonormal vectors (-1,2)/√5 and (2,1)/√5 have eigenvalues 6 and 1, respectively. Thus PᵀP = I and PᵀAP = diag(6,1), giving Q = 6y_1²+y_2². The deliberately incorrect submission selected d.

content.knowledge_point: Reducing a Quadratic Function Over the 2D-Space to the Canonical Form Using Orthogonal Transformations
content.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
content.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +6 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =6,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 7
?

Given the quadratic form Q(x)=x12+12x1x2−4x22, find its canonical (diagonal) form yTDy and an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables.

a
D=[800−5] and P=[15−252515]
b
D=[800−5] and P=[12−121212]
c
D=[500−8] and P=[313−213213313]
d
D=[8005] and P=[12−121212]
e
D=[500−8] and P=[−213313313213]
Submit

decision.explanation: A = [[1,6],[6,-4]] has characteristic polynomial λ²+3λ-40 = (λ-5)(λ+8). The vectors (3,2)/√13 and (-2,3)/√13 are orthonormal eigenvectors with eigenvalues 5 and -8, respectively. Thus option c satisfies PᵀAP = D, giving Q = 5y_1²-8y_2².

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+12{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-4{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 6 \\ 6 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -40 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,-8\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 6 \\ 6 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-8)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]-(-8)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-8)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -8\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]
$$

content.knowledge_point: Reducing a Quadratic Function Over the 2D-Space to the Canonical Form Using Orthogonal Transformations
content.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+12{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-4{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
content.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 6 \\ 6 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -40 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,-8\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 6 \\ 6 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-8)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]-(-8)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-8)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -8\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]
$$
